The spokesperson, briefing journalists after police spent the day searching the scene, said authorities had not yet found the vehicle and were still trying to determine whether the breach was an accident or a crime In August, investigators discovered [USN:L8N4420RI TEXT:"an explosive-laden drone"] near a runway at the airport, an event that German officials later said [USN:L8N44T1P2 TEXT:"Russia was responsible"] for. Russia has denied the allegations One runway had been closed but was again operating, the police spokesperson said German police first responded to the breach late on Saturday evening Leipzig police said they had not found suspicious objects or unauthorized people Officers on Sunday could be seen inspecting the area around a large break in the chain-link and barbed-wire fence

item.title: Rubio arrives in Central Asia while other US officials hit foreign policy hot spots
item.description: While the Iran war smolders, Saudi Arabia fights the Houthis and a new rift opens in US-Ukraine relations, Secretary of State Marco Rubio traveled on Sunday to Uzbekistan, a nation far removed from the biggest US foreign policy challenges.
item.dc:creator: Gram Slattery, Simon Lewis
item.content:encoded: While the Iran war smolders, Saudi Arabia fights the Houthis and a new rift opens in US-Ukraine relations, Secretary of State Marco Rubio traveled on Sunday to Uzbekistan, a nation far removed from the biggest US foreign policy challenges. The top US diplomat landed in Samarkand on Sunday night to meet with top officials from the C5+1, a grouping that brings together the United States and the Muslim-majority post-Soviet states of Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan. US officials have portrayed resource-rich Central Asia — the region between China, Russia and Iran — as worthy of more attention than it received from US President Donald Trump's predecessors. Trump hosted C5 leaders at the White House last November, when Kazakhstan agreed to join the Abraham Accords, a series of agreements under which Muslim-majority countries have normalized or deepened relations with Israel. Separately, Trump met with Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev at the United Nations General Assembly in September of last year. Regional politics aside, the trip fits an emerging pattern in which Rubio often visits regions not at the center of the news cycle, while leaving some more fraught foreign policy portfolios to other Trump aides, including special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner and Vice President JD Vance. Rubio has not visited Kyiv or Moscow since becoming secretary of state and was not present for talks between US and Ukrainian officials in Florida earlier this month, when US officials pressed Ukraine to stop hitting Russian refineries. Vance, not Rubio, represented the US in Pakistan during peace talks with Iran in April. Rubio's previous foreign trip, in early October, took him to Greece, Portugal and Iceland. Trump administration officials have typically rejected any suggestion that cabinet-level officials should focus their travels on geopolitical capitals and hot spots. Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau, for instance, said on X last week that the idea only certain destinations were worthy of visits from secretaries of state "perfectly encapsulates the decadence and degeneracy of the contemporary US foreign policy establishment." Speaking to reporters before leaving Washington on Saturday, Rubio said the timing of the Uzbekistan trip was dictated in part by the availability of the various delegations. He also said that foreign trips were too often designed to resolve immediate issues rather than build long-term relationships. "I mean, one of the things that suffers is the strategic business," Rubio told reporters. "You're always visiting someplace where there's a crisis or there's a problem or ... you're going because there's a conference." US-RUSSIA RELATIONS LOOM The delegation that greeted Rubio upon his arrival in Samarkand included Uzbek Foreign Minister Bakhtiyor Saidov, whom Rubio embraced warmly. Two women in traditional Uzbek attire presented Rubio and his wife with bouquets. One Central Asian diplomat, speaking on the condition of anonymity, said officials in the region were wondering to what extent the US would continue targeting Russian sanctions evasion. All C5 states, while drawing closer to the US, have deep historical ties with Moscow, and the region has facilitated Russian imports and exports that violate US and European Union sanctions, Western officials say. In the past, the US has pushed regional states to clamp down on those illicit flows. But Trump struck a deal with Moscow this month to [USN:L1N45Y0GJ TEXT:"import Russian diesel"], aimed at lowering domestic fuel prices before congressional midterm elections. On Friday, Trump [USN:L1N463009 TEXT:"waived"] all provisions of legislation that would have allowed him to slap massive tariffs on some nations that buy significant amounts of Russian crude oil or otherwise help Moscow evade sanctions. Among the nations that could have been affected, experts have said, are India and Kazakhstan. India, which Rubio will visit after Uzbekistan, remains the world's No. 2 Russian crude importer after China, despite Trump saying in February that India had agreed to stop buying oil from Russia. Additional questions hang over a potential trade deal with India and an expansion of the Abraham Accords in Central Asia. A US official, speaking on the condition of anonymity, described the trade deal on Friday as "pretty much done," raising the possibility that an agreement could be announced during the Rubio trip. Separately, the US [USN:L1N3TQ0WH TEXT:"has talked to"] additional Central Asian nations about joining the Abraham Accords, Reuters reported last year, conversations that potentially could continue in Samarkand. More than 200 business executives are accompanying Rubio to Uzbekistan, the State Department said. The Central Asian diplomat said the Trump administration has focused its commercial efforts on expanding access to the area's rare earth mineral resources. After Uzbekistan, Rubio will visit the Indian cities of Mumbai and Jamnagar to meet with business leaders, including Reliance Industries (RELI.NS) Chairman Mukesh Ambani, who earned the Trump administration's favor earlier in the year by backing a new refinery in Texas. Rubio most recently visited India five months ago. The trip is due to wrap up on Thursday.

item.title: Rubio says Trump to take up to 60 days to weigh Russia sanctions
item.description: Ukraine's Zelenskiy says sanctions waiver will prolong war with Russia.
item.dc:creator: Nandita Bose, Gram Slattery
item.content:encoded: The day after waiving sanctions and tariffs related to Russian exports, US President Donald Trump said on Saturday he has yet to announce a final decision on the matter, while Secretary of State Marco Rubio said officials want more time to evaluate the situation. Rubio said on Saturday that the president will use up to 60 days to assess the economic impact of Russia-related sanctions and tariffs that he waived a day earlier. "A lot of you don't know what my decision is yet, but we'll figure it out, and you'll figure it out," Trump told reporters at his Mar-a-Lago club in Palm Beach, Florida. In a Truth Social post on Sunday, Trump wrote that his decision-making was aimed at avoiding anything "that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table." Trump signed an executive order on Friday waiving key sanctions and tariffs under the law known as the Graham Act, which he signed last month at the urging of lawmakers who want to pressure Moscow over its war in Ukraine. The measures, including tariffs on Russian goods and penalties on countries buying Russian oil and gas, were due to take effect next week. Friday's order did not specify how long the waiver would last, but Rubio said Trump opted for a 60-day review. "I think the president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyze what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the US economy," Rubio told reporters before boarding a plane for a trip to Uzbekistan. Friday's executive order [USN:L1N463009 TEXT:"drew criticism"] from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, who warned it would embolden Russian President Vladimir Putin and prolong the war. DIESEL SUPPLIES Rubio on Saturday also defended a separate US agreement with Russia to increase diesel supplies to global markets, aimed at easing fuel prices that have climbed amid the war with Iran and disruptions to energy supplies. "That diesel is going to be sold one way or the other," Rubio said. "The only difference is how much of it the United States was going to get." Under the agreement, Trump said Russia initially would supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel to the United States, followed by shipments in November and beyond. The diesel agreement is "a carrot to try to end the war, not an economic lifeline" to Russia, US Secretary of Energy Chris Wright said during a Sunday interview on ABC's "This Week." But "the only way they can get additional diesel to export is if they turn down the conflict with Ukraine," Wright told CNN's "State of the Union" program on Sunday. “If Russia can bring additional diesel to the market and export it, it would benefit American consumers,” he told CNN. “He's putting pressure that would both benefit American consumers and be a step forward for peace in the Russia-Ukraine war.” Rubio said the diesel deal and sanctions waiver reflected the challenge of managing conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine that have disrupted global energy supplies. "These conflicts around the world are starting to crash into each other," he said.

item.title: Saudi-led coalition says helicopter crash in Najran kills two crew members
item.description: A reconnaissance AH-6i helicopter crashed in the Najran region of Saudi Arabia, killing its two crew members, the Saudi-led coalition's spokesperson Major General Turki al-Maliki said in a statement on Sunday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: A reconnaissance AH-6i helicopter crashed in the Najran region of Saudi Arabia, killing its two crew members, the Saudi-led coalition's spokesperson Major General Turki al-Maliki said in a statement on Sunday. The helicopter crashed due to a technical malfunction in an area under the jurisdiction of the Saudi National Guard Ministry, the statement added. Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis released footage later on Sunday of what they said was a Saudi AH-6i helicopter being shot down by a missile while carrying out what they described as hostile activities near Najran. The footage did not clearly show the incident, and Reuters could not immediately verify the Houthis' claim. There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities. On Saturday, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said on X that the group had shot down a Saudi Apache helicopter near Najran. It was not clear if that referred to the same incident. Al-Maliki commented on Saree's post on Sunday with a photo of several Apaches lined up, saying: "You claim to have shot it down, but it will enter the battlefield soon." Separately, the Saudi civil defence said on Sunday that six people were injured after a projectile it said was fired by Houthis fell on a residential area in Najran. Najran has been hit by attacks from the Houthis in recent weeks as fighting between the coalition and the Yemen-based group escalated, with the [USN:L1N4620VJ TEXT:"Yemen conflict"] becoming another front in the US-led war with Iran .

item.title: Deaths confirmed after 'serious incident,' fire at Canada military base in Alberta
item.description: People were killed and injured in a serious incident that resulted in a fire on one of Canada's busiest military bases in Alberta, Defense Minister David McGuinty said on Saturday.
item.dc:creator: Amanda Stephenson
item.content:encoded: People were killed and injured in a serious incident that resulted in a fire on one of Canada's busiest military bases in Alberta, Defense Minister David McGuinty said on Saturday. "I'm saddened to share that there have been both fatalities and injuries as a result of an incident" at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, McGuinty told reporters in Ottawa. He did not say how many people were killed or injured, or what caused the "tragic" situation at the base in the east-central part of the province, about 210 km (130 miles) east of Edmonton. A major fire was still burning on Saturday evening, he said, adding: "I cannot recall an incident like this in recent memory." The Canadian military and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police are investigating the incident, McGuinty said. Prime Minister Mark Carney posted on social media that the national government was "working closely with the Government of Alberta and local authorities." CFB Wainwright had 1,310 military and civilian personnel stationed there as of 2021, according to census data. The town of Wainwright, population about 6,600, is just north of the base. The municipality posted on social media that the fire had crossed the base fence into the nearby district but no evacuation orders had been issued. General Jennie Carignan, the chief of Canada's Defense Staff, said on social media that the Canadian forces are fully engaged with federal, provincial and local authorities. "Our priority remains the welfare of our members, their families and their community," she said. (This story has been corrected to add the dropped word 'not' in paragraph 3.)

item.title: US wants Israel to 'crack down' on settler violence in West Bank, Rubio says
item.description: "We're very disturbed by those images and what we're seeing," Marco Rubio said.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: The United States wants Israel to do more to deter attacks committed by settlers in the West Bank, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Saturday. "We're very disturbed by those images and what we're seeing," Rubio said. "We've asked the Israelis and continue to ask them to crack down on that stuff." His comments to reporters came after the widespread dissemination of video showing multiple individuals attacking Heidi Levine, an American photojournalist with the Washington Post. Levine was one of at least two people injured in the Friday incident, which took place as Israeli settlers [USN:L6N46304S TEXT:"attacked"] Palestinian civilians. European diplomats and a French mayor also were attacked in the occupied West Bank, Belgium's foreign minister said. The US State Department, Rubio said, has inquired about the event that included Levine's attack. Rubio, who spoke to reporters before boarding a flight to Uzbekistan, said he expects to hear back from the US Embassy in Jerusalem by Sunday. Israeli settlers in the West Bank have been involved in at least 170 attacks on Palestinians since September 27, around the start of the annual olive harvest, according to Yesh Din, an Israeli settlements monitoring group.

item.title: What redistricting means for Tennessee voters
item.description: Redrawing the lines splits neighbors and groups them with people far away.
item.dc:creator: Ally J. Levine, Bianca Flowers, David Hood-Nuño
item.content:encoded: It’s a political fault line that leaves neighbors on both sides with less say. 9th District5th District The street outside Tammy Jo O'Neal's home has become a political boundary with big implications. The city of Memphis used to sit almost entirely in one congressional district. The new map splits O'Neal from neighbors across the street, each now belonging to districts with voters halfway across the state who have different needs and interests. O'Neal sees the new map as more than a split block. “There's this divide that's happening in our lives,not just in our districts.” District 5 District 9 Tammy Jo O’Neal sits for a portrait on the front porch of their home on Elzey Ave in Memphis, Tennessee, US, July 29, 2026. REUTERS/Seth Herald A citydivided By Bianca Flowers , David Hood-Nuño and Ally J. Levine Published Oct. 17, 2026 6:00 a.m. EDT What happens when congressional district lines are redrawn, splitting neighbors and grouping them with people far away Four years before the Memphis redistricting, Republicans used a similar strategy in drawing new maps for Nashville. They split the city, which had voted overwhelmingly Democratic for roughly 70 years, into three broader districts where Republicans can now easily prevail. Battles over redistricting have long been intertwined with racism and political power, particularly in southern states like Tennessee. Sixty-four years ago, a federal court found Tennessee diluted voting power in urban areas where majority Black voters lived and ordered the legislature to redraw its congressional districts. For decades, the Voting Rights Act of 1965 was a powerful tool for Black voters, particularly in the South, to challenge discrimination and protect political power among people of color to elect representatives who would advocate for their communities. The act significantly increased Black and Hispanic representation in Congress by curtailing certain redistricting practices, including splitting people of color among many districts or concentrating them in some districts to limit their impact in others. But those protections have been steadily weakened. In 2013, when Democrat Barack Obama was president, the Supreme Court’s decision on the Alabama case Shelby County v. Holder gutted a provision requiring federal approval before states change voting laws or political maps. In April, the court narrowed the Voting Rights Act further in Louisiana v. Callais , making it harder to challenge new maps that dilute the voting power of communities of color. The court essentially required such challenges to prove that districts were drawn intentionally to discriminate on the basis of race, and not for other reasons. Republicans argue their redistricting in Tennessee and elsewhere is about party politics, not race. They point out that Democrats regularly redraw districts in states they control to give their party easier election wins. Democrats have done the same in California, for example, said Steve Hickey, chair of the Republican Party in Williamson County, a popular suburban area south of Nashville. “This is part of a bigger game being played nationally, and I don’t think it’s fair to say that this was done to gut” the Voting Rights Act, he said. Redistricting in the United States is generally controlled by state legislatures, which adjust voter maps after the once-a-decade census. Both parties have historically used the process to help their candidates win future elections. In 2025, at the urging of President Donald Trump, Texas launched an unusual mid-decade redistricting drive as part of a broader Republican push to gain congressional seats in half a dozen states, including Tennessee. Democrats responded with their own partisan redistricting in California and attempts that faltered in other states. Civil rights activists say Tennessee’s congressional districts, all of which currently favor Republicans, are now a testing ground for dismantling voting rights protections across the United States. “This lack of competition spills over and has racial implications,” said John Geer, a political science professor at Vanderbilt University who conducts polling in Tennessee. Reuters sought to quantify the impact of redistricting on the voters of Tennessee, examining public funding, demographics and socioeconomic factors to show why it’s important to residents when a city is split up like this. MemphisDistrict 9Suburbs of NashvilleDistrict 5District 8District 9 Population by race, one dot per person Black residents White residents Other races and ethnicities Memphis has the largest Black population in Tennessee. The city of some 630,000 people is 63% Black. Memphis accounted for 78% of the former District 9’s population, making it the only majority-Black district in the state. Earlier this year, the Tennessee legislature drew new district lines, splitting Memphis and its Black communities into three separate districts. The pieces of the city are now grouped with rural and suburban Tennesseans in districts that reach halfway across the state. Note: “White” and “Black” are non-Hispanic. “Other races and ethnicities” combines Hispanic or Latino residents of any race with the non-Hispanic categories Asian alone, American Indian and Alaska Native alone, Native Hawaiian and Other Pacific Islander alone, Some Other Race alone, and Two or More Races. Sources: US Census Bureau (2020 census redistricting data; TIGER/Line boundaries); Tennessee Comptroller of the Treasury (2026 districts); All About Redistricting, Loyola Law School (2022 districts); State of Tennessee and the City of Memphis Engineering Division (city limits); Tennessee Department of Transportation (roads) Reuters spoke to more than 35 redistricting scholars, political analysts, civic leaders, political candidates and voters about the consequences of redistricting for the most vulnerable communities in Tennessee’s two biggest cities. Cities faced the biggest impact because rural areas were already represented by a Republican and continue to be so after the redistricting, albeit in districts with different demographics. Before redistricting, both Nashville and Memphis were overwhelmingly Democratic districts in an otherwise Republican state. In 2024, District 9, including most of Memphis, went 71% for Democrat Steve Cohen. In 2020, Jim Cooper, a Democrat, ran unopposed in Nashville’s District 5, winning more than 99% of votes cast. In 2022, the new District 5 flipped, with the Republican candidate winning 57%. Tennessee’s new maps have combined city, suburban and rural populations that have widely varying needs and political preferences. The residents of Nashville and Memphis, for instance, are far more likely to struggle with poverty, housing, public safety and related issues. Residents there could now struggle to elect Congress members who prioritize policies to address these issues, according to Odessa Kelly, executive director of Stand Up Nashville, a nonprofit community organization that advocates for racial and economic equality. She said Black voters in Nashville no longer felt they had someone to stand up for them in Congress, from federal funding going to the city to critical votes on bills that directly affect city residents. The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention developed the Social Vulnerability Index to gauge how well a community can withstand and recover from an emergency, and to identify which communities may need the most support. Shelby County, home to Memphis, ranks among the most vulnerable of Tennessee’s 95 counties on various indicators such as housing cost burden and lack of access to a vehicle. Memphis, Nashville residents rank higher in social vulnerability A US government index compares Tennessee communities on socioeconomic and demographic factors gauging their resilience to unexpected hardships. 25th 50th 75th 100th percentile Lower vulnerability Higher vulnerability Shelby County (Memphis) Minority status Racial or ethnic minority 100 Davidson County (Nashville) Housing and transportation In structures of 10+ units 97 No vehicle available 94 More people than rooms 60 Lives in group quarters 56 Mobile homes 0 Household characteristics Aged 17 and under 97 Single-parent household 96 Speaks English less than well 91 With a disability 9 Aged 65 and over 5 Socioeconomic status Housing cost burdened 100 Unemployed 86 No health insurance 76 Below 150% of poverty 50 No high school diploma (25+) 16 0 Chart showing where Shelby County and Davidson County rank among Tennessee’s 95 counties on 16 measures of the CDC’s Social Vulnerability Index, grouped into four themes, on a scale from the 0 to the 100th percentile with the other 93 counties as faint ticks. Both rank high on most measures — Shelby at the 100th percentile for racial or ethnic minority share and housing cost burden, Davidson at the 100th for apartments in large buildings and for people who speak English less than well. Both drop to the middle or bottom on poverty, the 50th percentile for Shelby and the 23rd for Davidson, and on residents aged 65 and over. Source: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry Social Vulnerability Index 2022 In 2024, just over a third of Tennessee voters picked Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris, and in 2020, Democrats won two congressional seats out of the state’s nine, carrying Nashville and Memphis. Now, every congressional district in Tennessee is considered “safe” for Republicans. Sandi Wells, a self-described “very conservative” voter from Williamson County, just outside Nashville, said it was “kind of odd” to group Memphis in the same district with parts of Williamson County 200 miles away. But she rejected the notion that districts should be drawn to protect Black voting power. “I don’t think we should have districts that are based on race,” she said. “I mean, that’s just ridiculous for anyone to even think that we should have that.” Shane Tinnin, a 52-year-old small business owner who maintains homes in both cities and has voted mostly for Democrats, understands that parties seek political power through redistricting but called the Memphis maps a particularly striking setback for Black political power. “In Nashville, it seemed really more like this is a political move,” he said, noting that it was not a Black-majority city. “When you do it in Memphis, where it’s an even more liberal district, but also a predominantly Black district, it just feels especially egregious to me.” Odessa Kelly, executive director at Stand Up Nashville, points to topics of focus for her and her team at a meeting in July. REUTERS/Seth Herald Volunteers for The Equity Alliance canvass through neighborhoods in Memphis to do “accountability” door knocks to speak with residents about elected officials following the GOP-led effort to redistrict the city. REUTERS/Seth Herald Securing funding Reuters examined how Nashville’s redistricting has impacted community project funding, under which lawmakers can seek federal money for local projects. Previously known as earmarks, community project funds returned to Congress with a more transparent process in fiscal year 2022 after a decade-long moratorium. A Reuters analysis found a dramatic shift in funding for Nashville after the city was split among three districts. Jim Cooper, a Democrat, steered most of the old 5th District’s project funding to Nashville in fiscal years 2022 and 2023. In the years since, only a small share of funding has gone toward projects in the city, including fiscal year 2027 requests still pending before Congress. Funding can vary greatly between representatives. Only John Rose, who currently represents the 6th District, has requested funding among the three members whose districts included Nashville after redistricting. Matt Van Epps and Andy Ogles have not pursued community project funding for their districts at all, arguing against such spending on principle. All three did not provide a comment or did not respond to a request to comment. Total Community Project Funding for districts that include Nashville After FY2023 FY2024 $18 mln $21 mln $2.5 mln Not Nashville $18 mln Nashville Nashville $3 mln $15.5 mln Before Two flow diagrams comparing Community Project Funds before and after redistricting. In the year before, when Nashville sat in a single district, District 5 received $18 million and $15.5 million of it went to Nashville, with $2.5 million going elsewhere. In the year after, with Nashville divided across three districts, Districts 5, 6 and 7 received $21 million between them but only $3 million reached Nashville, while $18 million went to areas outside the city. Note: Data show the total funding for districts that include Nashville. Before the 2022 redistricting, Nashville was contained in District 5. After, it was split between Districts 5, 6 and 7. Source: US Government Accountability Office The shift away from community funding jeopardized future funding for projects like public housing, healthcare centers, buildings for the two historically Black colleges in the city and public transportation in Nashville. For Memphis, a similar decline in earmark funding would be a big loss. Since 2022, District 9 Representative Steve Cohen, a Democrat, pulled in $52.6 million for projects based in Memphis, according to figures published by the US Government Accountability Office and the US House Committee on Appropriations. That’s 83% of all the community project funding for District 9 in that period. District 7 State capitol District 6 State House of Representatives The Tennessee State Capitol building and Legislative Plaza, which is undergoing construction. REUTERS/Seth Herald Another important role for a member of Congress is to act as a middleman between people in their district and the government, helping negotiate the bureaucracy of Washington. When Cooper represented Nashville, he fielded calls about immigration paperwork, passports, Medicare, Social Security checks and more, said Tennessee State Senator Charlane Oliver, who worked as a community liaison and communications staffer in Cooper’s congressional office from 2017 to 2019. “He would show up to the cookout, the fish fry, the parades, the meetings and the galas,” she said. That kind of interaction is harder if the representative does not have a local office. When Nashville was split, only one representative, Mark Green of District 7, kept an office near the center of the city. That office was closed when Van Epps took over the seat in 2025, leaving no offices within the city limits. Constituents in Nashville have to drive 36 miles on average to visit a congressional district office, a Reuters analysis found, compared with less than 10 miles when Cooper represented Nashville, the seat of Davidson County. Average trip to Congressional district office District 5 +39 miles after District 6 +17 mi District 7 +16 mi 0 10 20 30 40 50 miles 9 miles before redistricting A chart of the average driving distance for Nashville residents to their closest congressional district office, shown for each of the three districts the city is now split among. A dark bar common to all three marks the 9-mile average from when Nashville sat in a single district, flagged on the scale as “9 miles before redistricting.” A lighter bar extends past it to each district’s new average: District 5 adds 39 miles, reaching about 47; District 6 adds 17, reaching about 25; and District 7 adds 16, reaching about 24 miles. Note: Data shows the average driving distance for Nashville residents in each district to their closest district office. District 7’s offices are those open under Rep. Matt Van Epps, who won the seat after Mark Green resigned in 2025. Green kept an office in downtown Nashville; which put District 7’s average at 5 miles. That office no longer exists. Source: Reuters analysis of congressional district office locations Van Epps and the other two Republicans running this year in Nashville districts, Johnny Garrett and Charlie Hatcher, did not respond to Reuters requests for interviews for this story. Most city buses don’t operate far enough outside the city to visit a congressional district office in Cookeville, more than an hour’s drive away. Kyle Cook, who works in the public library, said Cooper’s office used to be just upstairs from his own in downtown Nashville. “Now, if I wanted to advocate just as a regular citizen for better busing, I would have to call this office in Cookeville and it’s just not the same kind of relationship,” Cook said. Who speaks for Memphis? Cohen represented Memphis for 19 years but stood down when new maps were passed, saying “these districts were drawn to beat me.” State Representative Justin Pearson, a progressive Democrat, is campaigning to represent the 9th District. Pearson gained national attention in 2023 when he was temporarily expelled from the Tennessee House, for what Republicans described as a breach of decorum when he joined a protest on gun control . Polls show him trailing Brent Taylor, a Republican state senator endorsed by President Donald Trump. But Pearson said Tennessee was “not a lost cause” for Democrats. In an interview with Reuters, Pearson described the Memphis redistricting as “one of the most significant political deprivations of Black political power and accessibility to the ballot since the end of Reconstruction in Tennessee.” Tennessee State Representative Justin Pearson stands for a portrait in the Cooper Young neighborhood in Memphis. REUTERS/Seth Herald Taylor has defended redistricting efforts in Tennessee as a “compliance measure” in response to the 2026 US Supreme Court ruling that he says prohibits the consideration of racial data when redrawing political boundaries. Asked about his top priorities in such a diverse district spanning downtown Memphis to rural Fayette County, Taylor pointed to inflation. “Everybody feels the pain right now,” he said. “When I filled up my car the other day, it was $112. People feel the pinch at the gas pump. They feel higher prices when they go to the grocery store. Everything we do costs more.” Civil Miller-Watkins, an eighth-grade math teacher in Fayette County who was drawn into District 9 and plans to vote for Pearson, said the needs of voters in her area differ from those in Memphis. Rural voters worry about access to broadband, ambulances, grocery stores and schools, she said. “All of these interests are very legitimate,” Miller-Watkins said. “But I don’t know if any community can say they’re going to have effective representation.” Pearson, the Democrat, says he’s campaigned in 15 counties that now come under the district and economic hardship is the common thread. “That’s hurting people who are working class in Memphis, just like it’s hurting farmers in Savannah, Tennessee,” he said. “We have a lot more in common.” Urban 96% Suburban 4% Shelby County 737,000 people live in an urban county in District 9 Tipton County 31,000 live in a suburban county District 9 After Urban 35% Suburban 27% Memphis Nashville Williamson 107k Shelby 269k people Rutherford 39k Maury 33k Memphis area Small towns 22% Bedford 50k Lincoln 35k McNairy 26k Giles 30k Hardeman 25k Marshall 34k Lawrence 44k Hardin 27k Wayne 16k Moore 7k Rural 16% Before redistricting Fayette 25k Two panels comparing the counties that make up Tennessee’s 9th Congressional District before and after the 2026 redraw, with each county drawn at an area proportional to its population. Before, the district is almost entirely one place: urban Shelby County, home to Memphis, fills the panel with roughly 737,000 people, beside a thin sliver for suburban Tipton County’s ~31,000. After, 767,872 people are spread across 15 counties in four groups. Urban counties make up 35% of the district; suburban counties comprise 27%, small towns 22% and rural counties 16%. Note: Counties are grouped by the National Center for Health Statistics urban–rural classification. “Large central metro” was renamed to “Urban”, “Large fringe metro” to “Suburban”, “Micropolitan” to “Small towns” and “Noncore” was renamed “Rural” in this graphic. Sources: US Census; NCHS Urban-Rural Classification Scheme; Tennessee Comptroller of the Treasury (2026 district); All About Redistricting, Loyola Law School (2022 district) Pearson said he was concerned that some voters were confused about which district they were in and that this could hurt turnout. Pearson’s advocacy for criminal justice reform and affordability has appealed to younger Democratic Party voters like 27-year-old Marko Jankov. But Jankov, who identifies as a Democratic Socialist, lives in a part of Memphis that was moved out of the 9th District and he said he was less motivated to vote for other Democrats when polls showed them unlikely to win. “They want to make it a psychological thing, where you think you can’t win,” Jankov said. The changes are exposing a rural-urban divide. Debby Gould, president of the non-partisan League of Women Voters of Tennessee, said voters of all backgrounds had concerns. “This is a time when we really have to strengthen urban-rural links and to come up with shared values,” she said. “Because rural voters are also feeling left out on this.” Hickey, the Williamson County Republican chair, said it was up to candidates to show they could work for all their constituents: “They’re going to have to put a lot of miles in their car.” Opening photo Elzey Avenue in Memphis, a dividing line between Congressional District 9 and Congressional District 5, following a Republican-led effort to redistrict Memphis. item.title: BOJ may need to tighten faster if inflation beats forecast, IMF says
item.description: The Bank of Japan is "doing the right thing" by normalising monetary policy and may need to raise interest rates faster if inflation rises more than expected, a senior International Monetary Fund official told Reuters.
item.dc:creator: Leika Kihara
item.content:encoded: The Bank of Japan is "doing the right thing" by normalising monetary policy and may need to raise interest rates faster if inflation rises more than expected, a senior International Monetary Fund official told Reuters. Japan must also clarify how it plans to fund its big spending plans and lay out a medium-term fiscal framework to ease market concerns about fiscal risks, said Krishna Srinivasan, director of the IMF's Asia and Pacific Department. "I would say that they are doing the right thing at this point," Srinivasan said on the BOJ's efforts to lift its policy rate towards levels deemed neutral to the economy. "If inflation rises faster than expected, you have to start tightening faster because you don't want inflation expectations to get un-anchored. It's data dependent," he said in an interview on Friday. The remarks came ahead of the BOJ's key policy meeting later this month, when it [USN:L4N45S011 TEXT:"could keep rates steady"] but drop hawkish hints that would reinforce dominant market expectations of a December hike. Inflationary pressures from the Middle East conflict and brisk AI-demand were among key themes discussed by policymakers gathering for this week's annual IMF meetings in Bangkok. BOJ Governor Kazuo Ueda, who attended the IMF meetings, said on [USN:L1N4620G5 TEXT:"Friday"] the central bank will focus on anchoring underlying inflation around its 2% target and won't tolerate any overshoot, stressing anew its resolve to continue raising interest rates. For Japan, a weak yen adds to factors pushing up inflation by boosting the cost of raw material imports. Such mounting price pressures prodded the BOJ to raise rates to a 31-year high of 1.25% in [USN:L1N459138 TEXT:"September"], following a hike in June. Many analysts expect another rate increase by year-end. Japan also conducted a rare, coordinated intervention with the US on [USN:L1N43Z05E TEXT:"July 31"] to prevent the currency's slide to near 40-year lows from destabilising financial markets. In staff analysis included in its report on Asia's economy, the IMF said a big portion of yen moves since mid-2025 had little to do with fundamental factors such as yield differentials, and instead co-moved with speculative positions in yen futures. "Japan has a deep foreign exchange market, so as a first line of defense, they have allowed the exchange rate to move," Srinivasan said. "Bottom line, I would say that the Japanese authorities are fully committed to a freely floating exchange rate. I've had many discussions with them. So I don't doubt that at all," he said when asked if the recent yen intervention was justified. FISCAL FRAMEWORK NEEDED Rising global bond yields have also drawn attention at this week's IMF meetings as debt in advanced economies, including Japan, expanded after years of heavy spending. Markets worry that Japan may add to its already huge debt pile with the administration's big spending plans and a two-year cut to the consumption tax from April next year. Srinivasan said Japan has in fact seen fiscal consolidation proceed more than any other G7 country since the pandemic due in part to rising tax revenues. "Markets are concerned about the fiscal risks because of the uncertainty" on how Japan would pay for the fresh spending and tax-cut plans, he said. "Japan also would benefit from having a medium-term fiscal framework."

item.title: CoreWeave's CEO sold nearly $1 billion of stock since IPO, filings show
item.description: The sales began about two months after the stock hit a record high in June 2025.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: CoreWeave (CRWV.O) CEO Michael Intrator and entities linked to him have sold nearly $1 billion of stock, mostly under prearranged trading plans, since the AI cloud company's IPO in March last year, according to regulatory filings. The sales began about two months after the stock hit a record high in June 2025. The shares have tumbled since and were on track to lose about 24% this week [USN:L4N4620ZT TEXT:"as investors worried about"] the Nvidia-backed company's heavy capital spending and the debt needed to fund it amid rising bets on interest-rate hikes. CoreWeave did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment. Here are some more details: The sales totaled more than 10 million shares, according to the filings. As of Thursday's close, CoreWeave had a valuation of $38.44 billion. The sales were made by Intrator and affiliated entities such as Omnadora Capital, where Intrator serves as managing member, and two trusts. Most of these sales, excluding roughly $40 million, were made under prearranged trading plans that allow executives to sell shares on a preset schedule, and do not necessarily reflect management's view of the business. The roughly $40 million that was not part of prearranged plans was sell-to-cover sales, where shares were sold on the market to pay taxes on vested stock. The selling occurred as CoreWeave rapidly expanded its data-center footprint and increased spending on Nvidia chips to meet demand for AI computing, while building a revenue backlog of [USN:L6N4590TM TEXT:"more than $129 billion"]. In August, the company raised its annual capital expenditure forecast to be between [USN:L4N4481ER TEXT:"$35 billion and $39 billion"].

item.title: Hedge funds bet Japan reforms have further to run at Sohn Tokyo
item.description: The next phase of Japanese corporate reform took center stage at the Sohn Conference in Tokyo, as hedge fund managers highlighted investment opportunities ranging from a financial conglomerate's capital allocation strategy to an X-ray scattering firm's AI solutions.
item.dc:creator: Summer Zhen, Rocky Swift
item.content:encoded: The next phase of Japanese corporate reform took center stage at the Sohn Conference in Tokyo, as hedge fund managers highlighted investment opportunities ranging from a financial conglomerate's capital allocation strategy to an X-ray scattering firm's AI solutions. At the inaugural Sohn Conference in Japan, which invited 14 funds to pitch their top investment ideas, more than half of the investors favored the theme of corporate reform. Daisuke Nakayama, a portfolio manager at Hong Kong-headquartered Polymer Capital, picked Orix Corporation , a financial services firm, saying the change in management marks "a big turning point" for the company's transformation into a global investment firm. "The new leadership has a greater focus on capital allocation and ROE," Nakayama said, adding the firm is now using overseas capital, including from Qatar Investment Authority, to bid for companies. The number of activist campaigns in Japan hit a record last year, according to brokerage Jefferies, after years of pressure from regulators and the Tokyo Stock Exchange on companies to improve shareholder returns and invest in growth. BEYOND DIVIDENDS AND BUYBACKS Fund managers said that the next chapter is not just about companies increasing dividends and buybacks but also about focusing on those deploying capital to expand businesses and drive long-term growth. One example is Rigaku (268A.T) , an X-ray equipment supplier pivoting to semiconductor metrology, measuring and inspecting chips. New York-based Indus Capital Partners said it had invested in the company and had engaged with the firm to sell a stake to a US semiconductor firm to drive revenue. As semiconductor companies are going into vertical structures to scale, X-ray is needed to detect defects deeper in the 3D chips, said Byron Gill, managing partner at Indus. Rigaku might be one of the few companies that "has the key to unlocking scale for the semiconductor industry in the middle of a super cycle", he added, forecasting a 100% rise in its valuation by 2029. REFORM THEME DOMINATES The corporate reform theme still has a long way to run, market participants said. "Japan changes slowly, but once the change starts, it does not reverse," said Naohide Une, partner and CEO at Investment Lab, a former senior managing director at Japan Post Bank. He picked Japanese chemical company Ube Corporation (4208.T) for its corporate reform efforts. In a separate Q&A session, Seth Fischer, founder of activist Oasis Management, said his fund may substantially increase its stake in Japanese electric motor maker Nidec (6594.T) . AI AS A BACK-OFFICE TAILWIND AI was another key investment theme. Investment firms Ruane Cunniff and Japan Catalyst picked software companies Money Forward (3994.T) and OBIC Business Consultants (4733.T) , respectively. They argued that back-office software operators are AI winners rather than losers, as clients require accuracy. And these businesses are helping Japan overcome labor tightness, they said.

item.title: Why CoreWeave's troubles are rattling the AI boom
item.description: CoreWeave's mounting debt is raising concerns about the AI boom, as investors question whether demand can justify the billions being borrowed to build data centers.
item.dc:creator: Anhata Rooprai, Aditya Soni
item.content:encoded: CoreWeave's (CRWV.O) mounting debt is raising fresh concerns about the AI boom, as investors question whether demand can justify the billions being borrowed to build data centres. Shares and bonds of the Nvidia-backed (NVDA.O) company [USN:L4N46112V TEXT:"have tumbled"] despite its CEO's assurances of a strong contract backlog, fueling a broader selloff in technology stocks. Here is why investors are worried and what its troubles could mean for the industry. WHAT DOES COREWEAVE DO? CoreWeave rents out computing power from Nvidia processors to companies developing and running AI, including Microsoft (MSFT.O) and OpenAI. It is one of the leading "neocloud" providers, a group of newer cloud companies that are growing rapidly to meet demand for scarce and expensive AI chips. These neocloud companies give customers access to computing power without requiring them to build their own data centers. However, supplying such capacity requires heavy upfront investment in chips and infrastructure, often financed with debt. WHAT IS ITS FINANCIAL SITUATION? The company, which has never turned a profit, has about $50 billion in debt, according to data compiled by LSEG. It raised its annual capital spending forecast by $4 billion in August [USN:L4N4481ER TEXT:"to between $35 billion and $39 billion"]. Analysts expect revenue of nearly $13 billion this year and a loss of $2.13 billion. The yields on its bonds due in 2031, which are rated junk, have spiked to about 16%, while the cost of insuring its debt against default has climbed to about 1,000 basis points, reflecting growing concern among creditors. CEO Mike Intrator told employees in an internal memo seen by Reuters that its deal backlog more than covers its debt obligations. The company had a $104.2 billion revenue backlog at the end of the second quarter, followed by [USN:L6N4590TM TEXT:"more than $25 billion"] in new commitments early in the third quarter. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has also downplayed the concerns, saying CoreWeave's financial strength is improving and he sees no need to backstop it. The chip giant has agreed to buy unsold CoreWeave capacity through April 2032. WHY IT COULD BE A CANARY IN THE COAL MINE CoreWeave's business depends on two things: demand for AI computing and lenders' willingness to finance the infrastructure supplying it. But a selloff in its shares suggests a lack of confidence among investors in the latter, even as the company cites strong demand. The concern is not that AI demand will collapse, but that higher borrowing costs could make the business harder to sustain if demand were to weaken sharply. "It looks more like investors questioning how the build-out is being funded than a sudden collapse in appetite for AI computing," said Axel Rudolph, chief technical analyst at IG Group. "CoreWeave is quickly becoming the AI trade's canary in the coal mine," said Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB. WHY ARE MARKETS FRETTING? Investors are questioning whether AI revenue can grow fast enough to cover the cost of building and financing the infrastructure. CoreWeave has to spend heavily upfront before it can collect the revenue from its contracts. Higher interest rates could drive up financing costs and further squeeze returns. The hardware itself poses another risk. Chips lose value as newer generations arrive, pushing providers to spend even more to replace them. The concerns, however, go beyond CoreWeave. US technology giants are expected to spend more than $700 billion on AI infrastructure this year. THE DOWNSIDE SCENARIO One potential consequence would be a broader financing squeeze, with lenders demanding higher returns or becoming less willing to fund other AI projects. That could force providers to scale back expansion, curbing equipment purchases and affecting the computing capacity customers expect. A setback could also deepen doubts that the AI investment frenzy is outpacing returns, piling further pressure on technology stocks. The impact of the fallout would depend on how the business is reorganized, and CoreWeave's ties to major technology companies do not, by themselves, mean its failure would trigger a wider financial crisis. WHO ELSE BEARS THE RISK? Gartner estimates about 80% of neoclouds could shut down by 2030, warning that expected AI revenue will not support profitable returns on all planned infrastructure spending. Neocloud rivals Nebius (NBIS.O) , Applied Digital (APLD.O) and Iren (IREN.O) have fallen in the recent selloff. The cost of default protection has risen for SoftBank (9984.T) , which is betting heavily on OpenAI. Meanwhile, spreads for Amazon (AMZN.O) , Alphabet (GOOGL.O) , Meta (META.O) and Nvidia have also reached records, although they have risen much more slowly than CoreWeave's. However, these companies also have larger cash flows and stronger balance sheets.

item.title: AI credit worries send default insurance to record high
item.description: Investors rushed to hedge against the risk of credit stress building in the AI trade.
item.dc:creator: Tom Westbrook, Amanda Cooper
item.content:encoded: The cost of insuring against tech defaults struck record highs on Thursday, as investors rushed to hedge against the risk of credit stress building in the AI trade, with heavily indebted data centre operators like CoreWeave (CRWV.O) hit hardest. Hotter-than-expected [USN:L1N45Z121 TEXT:"US inflation data"], together with mounting expectations for higher interest rates, are adding to concerns about how quickly massive investment in artificial intelligence will translate into profits, as well as whether heavily indebted companies can generate returns fast enough to service mounting interest costs. Credit default swaps (CDS) are sending a warning signal to markets. The standouts were five-year CDS spreads for CoreWeave (CRWV.O) , which blew past 1,100 bps, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence data , while the yield on the company's 2031 bond rose to as much as 16% before retreating to around 14%. Cloud computing giant Oracle (ORCL.N) , which has also stirred up investor angst because of its vast borrowing, saw its CDS near 300 bps, bringing the rise this week to around 31 bps. CDS for Nvidia (NVDA.O) , Franco-Italian chipmaker STMicroelectronics and SpaceX (SPCX.O) , which offers some AI services, rose sharply. CoreWeave, a loss-making "neocloud" company that owes nearly $50 billion, according to LSEG data, is in the eye of the storm. "CoreWeave is quickly becoming the AI trade’s canary in the coal mine," said Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB. "Its bonds have sold off sharply ... this is a sign that investors might be going off the AI investment narrative, which has included massive debt issuance to fund AI ambitions." A surge in quarterly revenue from [USN:L6N4601AA TEXT:"AI developer Anthropic"] did little to calm the market's nerves. According to an investor who attended a pre-IPO meeting with the company's leadership in San Francisco on Wednesday, third-quarter revenue rose 45% to $16.8 billion from the previous quarter. Anthropic is targeting a valuation of $2 trillion. DEBT MARKET JITTERS CDS spreads show the number of basis points charged for default protection. The greater the perceived risk of a credit event, the wider the spread, meaning the 1,000 bps for CoreWeave CDS implies a risk of default in the coming five years of 64%, up from around 30% a year ago. Earlier this week, [USN:L1N45Z07U TEXT:"Broadcom Chief Executive"] Hock Tan compared the investor rush for anything AI-related to "casino gambling." CoreWeave stock was down another 2% on Thursday, following a 15% slide on Wednesday, meaning nearly a fifth of the company's value has burned up in two days. CoreWeave shares have now fallen 10% since the start of this year, while those of rival Nebius (NBIS.O) , for which there are no publicly tradable CDS, are up about 114%. Credit default swap spreads for Amazon (AMZN.O) , Alphabet (GOOGL.O) and Meta (META.O) also traded at record highs, data from LSEG and S&P Global Market Intelligence showed, though they have risen far more slowly than Oracle, or CoreWeave. "This is not the first time we’ve had a sizeable market wobble on the back of AI fears, but as we move to a capex cycle funded out of debt rather than simply free cash flow, we have to increasingly respect the credit price action. AI financing costs aren’t dramatic overall, but there are worrying themes at the edges," Deutsche Bank strategist Jim Reid said.

item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Trump dispose d'un délai pour se prononcer sur les sanctions contre la Russie, dit Rubio 17 octobre (Reuters) - Le secrétaire d'Etat américain Marco Rubio a déclaré samedi que Donald Trump disposait d'un délai pouvant aller jusqu'à 60 jours pour évaluer l'impact économique des sanctions et des droits de douane liés à la Russie. L'Egypte prête à contribuer à la sécurité de l'Arabie saoudite 18 octobre (Reuters) - L'Egypte est prête à apporter à l'Arabie saoudite le soutien nécessaire à la défense de sa sécurité et de sa stabilité face aux attaques des Houthis, a déclaré dimanche la présidence égyptienne. Première apparition publique du pape depuis son opération pour un cancer du poumon CITE DU VATICAN, 18 octobre (Reuters) - Le pape Léon XIV a promis dimanche de reprendre progressivement ses fonctions à la tête de l'Eglise catholique lors de sa première apparition publique depuis son opération subie il y a cinq jours pour un cancer du poumon. Les USA ont repris le partage de renseignements avec l'Ukraine, dit Zelensky 18 octobre (Reuters) - Les États-Unis ont repris le partage de renseignements avec l'Ukraine pour l'aider à se défendre contre les attaques de missiles russes, a déclaré dimanche le président Volodimir Zelensky. Trump apporte son soutien à Netanyahu pour les élections en Israël WASHINGTON, 18 octobre (Reuters) - Le président américain Donald Trump a apporté dimanche son soutien à Benjamin Netanyahu en vue des prochaines élections législatives israéliennes. Un ministre russe au FMI boycotté par les Européens Plusieurs délégués du comité de pilotage du Fonds monétaire international (FMI) ont quitté samedi une réunion au moment où le ministre russe des Finances, Anton Silouanov, prenait la parole, rapportent trois sources présentes. Vaste manifestation à Tunis contre le président Saïed Des milliers de personnes ont manifesté samedi à Tunis contre le président Kaïs Saïed, l'accusant de saper la démocratie et l'économie du pays. Le pape Léon XIV est sorti de l'hôpital Le pape Léon XIV est sorti de l'hôpital samedi après-midi pour regagner le Vatican, quatre jours après avoir subi une intervention chirurgicale pour un cancer du poumon. Zelensky dénonce de nouvelles restrictions imposées par Starlink L'Ukraine n'est pas en mesure d'utiliser ses systèmes d'interception contre les attaques de drones russes en raison de restrictions de vitesse imposées par Starlink, a déclaré samedi le président ukrainien Volodimir Zelensky, ajoutant que Kyiv discutait de cette question avec des responsables américains. Des Palestiniens et des responsables européens attaqués par des colons en Cisjordanie occupée TAYBEH, Cisjordanie, 17 octobre (Reuters) - Des colons juifs masqués ont attaqué des Palestiniens, des représentants de l'Eglise catholique et des responsables européens en Cisjordanie occupée, a annoncé samedi le ministre belge des Affaires étrangères.

item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: France-Macron dénonce la violence débridée et promet des aides PARIS, 18 octobre (Reuters) - Le président Emmanuel Macron a dénoncé dimanche la "violence débridée de factieux de la mouvance d'ultra-gauche et de délinquants", tout en appelant les Français en général et les partis politiques en particulier au dialogue et au sens de la responsabilité. 855 interpellations samedi à Paris, décès d'un manifestant d'un arrêt cardiorespiratoire - préfecture PARIS, 18 octobre (Reuters) - Un manifestant est décédé à la suite d'un arrêt cardiorespiratoire samedi à Paris lors des manifestations contre la vie chère, pendant lesquelles 855 interpellations ont été effectuées, ce qui représente un "chiffre record", a déclaré dimanche la préfecture de police. Paris condamne l'agression d'un maire français par des colons juifs PARIS, 18 octobre (Reuters) - La France a condamné dimanche l'agression "gravissime" par des colons juifs du maire d'Aulnoye-Aymeries survenue la veille dans le village palestinien de Taybeh. France et Allemagne d'accord sur un plan pour l'automobile La France et l'Allemagne ont annoncé vendredi un accord sur une "approche commune" visant à garantir l'avenir de l'industrie automobile européenne, avec un accent mis à la fois sur la transition énergétique et sur une production des véhicules en Europe. Les tortues caouannes, sentinelles du réchauffement en Méditerranée Sous un ciel baigné de lune, des bébés tortues sortent du sable sur la côte méditerranéenne turque et se hâtent vers la mer, dans un cycle naturel ancestral de plus en plus menacé par le changement climatique. Une étoile verte récemment découverte émerveille les astronomes Pour la première fois, des astronomes ont identifié une étoile verte, un vestige stellaire dense appelé "naine blanche", qui a pris une teinte fantomatique de vert chartreuse après avoir absorbé des débris rocheux provenant de planètes qui, autrefois, gravitaient autour d’elle. La santé du pape Léon en "amélioration constante", dit le Vatican Le pape Léon XIV continue de se remettre de son intervention chirurgicale subie mardi pour un nodule cancéreux au poumon, a déclaré vendredi le Vatican, soulignant "l'amélioration constante" de son état de santé. Le pape Léon XIV se rétablit comme prévu de son opération d'un cancer du poumon Le rétablissement du pape Léon XIV de son opération d'un cancer du poumon suit son cours, a annoncé jeudi le Vatican, qui précise que le souverain pontife de 71 ans a recommencé à travailler. Les dirigeants de l'UE se réunissent en sommet, tensions en vue sur le budget Les chefs d'Etat et de gouvernement de l'Union européenne se réunissent jeudi à Bruxelles pour un sommet lors duquel devraient être mises en exergue les divergences sur l'ampleur du prochain budget pluriannuel et sur les priorités de dépense du bloc communautaire, sans accord attendu dans l'immédiat. Macron va effectuer une tournée dans le Golfe, sécurité et énergie au menu Emmanuel Macron effectuera en début de semaine prochaine une tournée dans le Golfe afin de "poursuivre sa mobilisation" auprès de dirigeants régionaux pour revenir à la stabilité et à la libre circulation dans le détroit d'Ormuz, voie cruciale pour les livraisons énergétiques mondiales, a dit mercredi l'Elysée.
